fields.oneLiner: ArticleClock builds a CA articleship student's week around the hours he actually has left after office, and moves the plan when audit season eats a Saturday.
fields.jobStory:
When an articled assistant gets back to his PG at 9.40pm after a statutory audit day that ran long, he wants tomorrow's study plan to have already adjusted itself, so I can keep a CA Final subject moving instead of opening a plan made in June that assumed he had four free hours every evening.

Who has this job: second and third year CA articled assistants in Jaipur and Ahmedabad who are simultaneously working 50 to 70 hour weeks at a mid-size firm and preparing for CA Final. They sit in the same four or five firms, they are all in the ICAI branch student WhatsApp groups, and they show up at the same two libraries near Malviya Nagar on Sundays. I interviewed nine of them and sat with three while they showed me their plans.

What they do instead: a Notion template bought from an Instagram page for 199 rupees, or a paper timetable stuck inside a cupboard. All nine had made a plan. Seven had abandoned it inside three weeks, and every one of them gave the same reason: the plan assumed evenings that audit season took away, and once you are four days behind, re-drawing the whole plan is itself an evening you do not have.
fields.trafficTestNotes:
Two sources over eight days, 3 to 11 September 2026.

1. Instagram. I made three reels about the abandoned-timetable problem on a new account and posted 3, 6 and 9 Sep. Insights show 8,900, 2,100 and 14,600 accounts reached, so about 25,600 total. The link is in the bio. The bio link short URL shows 194 clicks. Most of the signups came from the third reel, the one where I filmed an actual abandoned paper timetable inside a cupboard.

2. The ICAI Jaipur branch students WhatsApp group, roughly 380 members, posted once on 7 Sep with permission from an admin. 41 clicks from that link.

So about 235 visits from 25,980 reach, and 25 signups, which is around 10.6%. Spend was zero, I did not boost anything, the only cost was my time editing three reels. I would not read too much into 10.6% because the reel that worked was very specific to one complaint, so the people clicking were already nodding along before they reached the page.

notes: Return: a flat contradiction. The write-up reports 25 signups, the dated Google Forms screenshot says 3 responses with three rows. Everything else - one-liner, job story, audience, live page, named sources with reach, visits and zero spend - clears the bar, so the whole return rests on evidence consistency and this is the kind of mismatch the bar says goes to a human rather than passing quietly.
